substeps.caption: An example run on the alloy line: a build plate from the Aconity MIDI, through a depowdering box, to the wire EDM, which cuts the tensile bars off it, then one bar, rinsed and dried, to the Instron. The UR10e rides its MiR250 along the fronts.

The print is done: four ASTM E8 subsize tensile bars, 100 mm long and 6 mm thick, printed flat in AlSi10Mg on a 170 mm plate (DAL PR #169's build at Utah), and a handling lug for the gripper. They are still buried in the powder. The chamber is drawn see-through.

The chamber door opens and the MiR250 rolls up. The MIDI has no automatic depowdering, so the arm takes a suction lance off its post beside the chamber. A pipe along the floor takes what it picks up to the depowdering box's separator, in the gap between the printer and the Instron.

Into the depowdering box beside the printer: the door slides up and the arm sets the plate's stud in a zero-point chuck on a turning shaft. The box is our design, on the principle of Solukon's SFM-AT200, the smallest made for this (plates to 300 × 300 × 230 mm, 60 kg), which would need about a metre more of line.

The crosshead comes down until the upper grip takes the bar's other end, 40 mm of it free between the jaws, and the upper grip closes.

The test: the crosshead pulls at a constant rate and the load cell reads the force. The curve is not a measurement: it runs through AddUp's published as-built values (AddUp AlSi10Mg data sheet, as built, XY, ASTM E8). The bar breaks at about 412 MPa, 5 % strain, with little necking.
Broken. The crosshead backs off 20 mm to show the break; the halves go on to the SEM for fractography.
Done: printed, depowdered, cut, rinsed and tested, every arm move a real one, and no step left to a person. The depowdering box and the rinse cup are new stations of our own design.
